summary: Defines Attribute-Value Pair containers for several priority parameters in Diameter and the AAA framework. The parameters themselves come from several protocols operating at either the network or application layer. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Some messages are more urgent than others. This memo defines labeled boxes in Diameter where you can put an urgent sign that came from other systems.

questions: how to carry priority in diameter
subtitle: Diameter containers that carry priority values taken from RSVP and SIP resource-priority mechanisms.

tldr.problem: Priority parameters are defined in other protocols, such as RSVP and SIP, and a Diameter server that authorizes a user's QoS had no standard way to hand those values to the network.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6735 defines AVPs (codes 608 to 617) that mirror the priority fields of RSVP and SIP Resource-Priority, for use with the Diameter QoS application.
tldr.outcome: The AVPs only carry and validate values. Neither they nor Diameter perform or realize QoS; local policy decides how the values are used.

today: RFC 6735 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2012, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the metadata. It stays the reference for these Diameter priority AVPs.

sections.title: Why Carry Priority in Diameter
sections.content:
This RFC defines Attribute-Value Pairs (AVPs) for the Diameter protocol (RFC 6733) that convey a specific set of priority parameters. The parameters themselves are specified in other documents. The AVPs are extensions to those in RFC 5866, and the priority fields they mirror are extensible and allow values beyond those already defined or registered with IANA.

Priority influences how resources are distributed and so the QoS a flow receives. The influence may be probabilistic, between but not including 0% and 100%, or it may be a guarantee to receive or not receive the resource.

The RFC also notes AVPs defined by the 3GPP, such as Reservation-Priority and Session-Priority, which are aimed at IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS) environments and are viewed as private implementations in a walled garden. The AVPs here are not constrained to IMS, and how the two families coexist is left for further study.
sections.plainLanguage: Some network traffic, like an emergency call, deserves to go first. This memo gives Diameter a standard place to write down how important a flow is.

sections.title: What the Priority AVPs Do and Do Not Do
sections.content:
The AVPs are for use with the Diameter QoS application (RFC 5866) and continue the list of AVPs begun in RFC 5624. Each one corresponds to a priority field in another protocol, and the value it holds is the same value that field would hold there.

The RFC stresses that neither these AVPs nor Diameter perform or realize the QoS for a session or flow of packets. They are part of a mechanism to determine validation of the priority value.
sections.plainLanguage: These boxes are like a note saying how important a package is. The note does not move the package faster; it only tells whoever is in charge.

sections.title: RSVP-Derived AVPs
sections.content:
The Dual-Priority AVP (code 608) is a grouped AVP made of Preemption-Priority (609) and Defending-Priority (610). Both are Unsigned16, and higher values mean higher priority. They come from the Signaled Preemption Priority Policy Element (RFC 3181) of RSVP (RFC 2205). In that element the defending priority is set when a reservation is admitted. A new request's preemption priority is compared with the defending priority of an admitted flow, and the action taken is a function of local policy.

The Admission-Priority AVP (611) is of type Unsigned8. It is used to increase the probability of session establishment for selected RSVP flows, higher values meaning higher priority, and it is encoded with the same value as the admission-priority parameter in Section 5.1 of RFC 6401.
sections.plainLanguage: One pair of numbers says how strongly a new flow can push others out and how strongly an existing flow holds its seat. Another number says how likely a flow is to get in the door at all.

sections.title: SIP and Application-Level Resource Priority
sections.content:
The SIP-Resource-Priority AVP (612) is grouped from a namespace AVP (613) and a value AVP (614), both UTF8String. They are derived from the Resource-Priority header field of RFC 4412: the namespace identifies a unique ordered set of priority values, and the value names a member of that set.

The Application-Level-Resource-Priority (ALRP) AVP (615) is grouped from ALRP-Namespace (616) and ALRP-Value (617). RFC 6401 modifies the RFC 4412 registry to assign numerical values to namespaces and priority values. The SIP and ALRP AVPs therefore convey the same priority semantics with different syntax: alphanumeric strings in the former, numeric-only values in the latter.
sections.plainLanguage: The same priority can be written in words or in numbers. One box takes the words used by phone-call software, and the other takes the matching numbers.

sections.title: Example of Usage
sections.content:
In the RFC's scenario, a user with special authorization is authenticated by a Network Access Server (NAS), which is a client of a Diameter server. The server returns the user's authorized QoS, including Dual-Priority, Admission-Priority and/or ALRP AVPs. Local policy at the NAS decides whether the flow can be admitted. If so, the NAS forwards the values in RSVP signaling, and each later node makes its own decision, again under local policy.

Local policy might say which value wins if both Admission-Priority and ALRP are present, which namespaces are recognized, and which resources can be preempted if the Dual-Priority values are high enough.

For SIP-Resource-Priority the first decision point is typically a SIP proxy that receives a request with a Resource-Priority header field. It compares that header with the AVP content from the Diameter server, and may then map the header to numeric values from RFC 6401 to signal an RSVP border router.
sections.plainLanguage: A visitor shows a special pass at the front desk. The desk asks the head office what the pass allows, then tells each next desk, and every desk still follows its own house rules.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document follows the security considerations of the Diameter QoS application (RFC 5866) and of Diameter itself (RFC 6733). It recommends integrity mechanisms when values move between protocols, for example S/MIME with the SIP Resource Priority Header or an INTEGRITY object within an RSVP POLICY_DATA object. Altered values could lead to more or fewer resources being allocated.

Changes in integrity-protected values SHOULD NOT be ignored, and appropriate protocol-specific errors SHOULD be sent upstream. The text deliberately does not say MUST NOT, because the local policy of an administrative domain is the final arbiter, and some deployments sit inside a single domain or walled garden.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone changes the importance note on a package, you might give it too much or too little room. So the note should be sealed, and if the seal is broken you should usually say so.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA allocated AVP codes 608 to 617 for the AVPs defined here. It also allocated a new value in the QoS Profiles subregistry created by RFC 5624: the profile named Resource priority parameters, with value 1.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry keeper reserved ten code numbers for the new boxes and one name tag for this whole set.
